Facts:
[1] Tracking categorized by what tracked into three: sense organs, other body parts, surrounding environment not related to user.
[2] Sense organs (eyes/ears) tracked because body-controlled DOF and display attached must be perceived attached to surrounding world, so position/orientation tracked to update virtual world/UX.
[3] In VR, sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, sufficient for visual/aural components related eyes/ears.
[4] In VR, eye tracking may be required if rendering/display require compensating for eye movements, and may be part of head tracking.
[5] Other body parts required when user wants representation of body in virtual world, avatars/virtual hands, may involve facial expressions/hand gestures for interaction, motion reproduced in virtual world's matched zone.
[6] For other body parts, perfect matching not required; approximate movement/representation can provide good experience.
[7] Limiting case: send simple explicit input signal, e.g. button press, to change to predetermined body configuration, e.g. virtual hand grasp object, without elaborate tracking.
[8] Surrounding environment not related to user may involve tracking physical objects in real world around user; more important in AR but also important in VR.
[9] In AR, moved physical object must be tracked in real-world view so digital content appropriately registered in 3D space.
[10] In VR, tracking environment can alert user to physical objects not represented in virtual world, such as wall, to reduce harm; tracking user not useful, environment itself must be tracked.
[11] In VR, tracked physical objects may be matched in virtual world so user receives touch feedback while interacting, better natural experience.
[12] Telepresence applications: large part of physical world brought into virtual world through live capture, augmenting virtual world with live capture; generally classified as augmented virtuality, form of tracking surrounding environment.

Facts:
[1] Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user.
[2] Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.
[3] In VR, sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.
[4] In VR, eye tracking may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movements, and eye tracking may be part of head tracking.
[5] Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone.
[6] For tracking of the user's other body parts, perfect matching is not required; approximate movement or an approximate representation of the body-part movement in the virtual world can provide a good experience.
[7] A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking.
[8] Tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user may involve tracking physical objects in the real world around the user; it is more important in AR, but also important in VR.
[9] In AR, a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in 3D space.
[10] In VR, tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, to reduce harm; for this, tracking the user is not useful, and the environment itself must be tracked.
[11] In VR, tracked physical objects may be matched in the virtual world so that the user receives touch feedback while interacting with them, giving a better, more natural experience.
[12] In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

[5] Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers.
